content: Collected plasma is not the sole source of plasma products in the country. Commercial plasma products are also procured through private sector channels and as part of state healthcare services. A binational agreement exists for the exchange of plasma and plasma-derived medicinal products (PDMPs) with the fractionation plant of the National University of Cordoba. For patients under the Administration of State Health Services (ASSE), albumin is provided with 100% coverage. In 2013, the plasma interchange program successfully fulfilled all treatment requests for ASSE patients requiring intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). In Bolivia, users of public and private healthcare systems are responsible for paying low-cost single fees approved by the Ministry of Health. For those in the social security system, contributions are made monthly. In Colombia, an obligatory health insurance plan ensures that certain procedures, including blood transfusions and the use of blood components, are covered by the system. In Zambia, the Zambia National Blood Transfusion Service (ZNBTS) is the sole entity authorized to collect blood from voluntary donors, process the donated units, and distribute them to user hospitals. The ZNBTS operates as a nationally coordinated system under the Ministry of Health. In Ghana, the national blood regulatory authority, the Food and Drugs Authority (FDA), is collaborating with the blood service to develop the necessary documentation for licensing and accrediting blood establishments. In Iran, the Iranian Blood Transfusion Organization (IBTO) is supervised by the High Council for all programs and activities. Evaluation and inspection by headquarters, along with High Council approval, are mandatory before centers can commence operations. Regular inspections of activities are conducted by the headquarters. In India, the National Accreditation Board for Hospitals and Healthcare Providers (NABH) has a specialized program for accrediting blood banks. In Sweden, county councils are responsible for funding and governing hospital blood banks (HBBs) and blood establishment entities (BEEs). These entities collaborate in an alliance and maintain regular communication with competent authorities. In South Africa, both the South African National Blood Service (SANBS) and the Western Province Blood Transfusion Service (WPBTS) publish formal annual reports detailing their activities and financial statements. In Italy, all blood services are accredited, and regular inspections are conducted to ensure compliance with national standards. In Costa Rica, a postgraduate program specializing in immunohematology and blood banking is offered by the University of Costa Rica. In Argentina, the Argentinian Association of Hemotherapy and Immunohematology (AAHI) collaborates with provincial ministries and universities to support blood transfusion services. In Jamaica, partial cost recovery is implemented, primarily from private hospitals. In the Philippines, funding for blood services is provided by the Ministry of Health, ensuring comprehensive coverage for blood safety and transfusion activities. In Uganda, a national blood policy and strategic plan for blood safety are in place, along with national standards for the collection, testing, processing, storage, and distribution of blood and blood components. In the Republic of Korea, a robust national hemovigilance system is operational, ensuring the collection of data on donorand recipient-related adverse events. In Ireland, all blood transfusion services are accredited, and regular inspections are conducted to maintain high standards of safety and quality. In Venezuela, the national blood service is self-financed through fees for blood products and laboratory services, with state involvement in staff salaries and equipment procurement. In Iceland, all blood services are accredited under ISO 9001:2008 standards, ensuring compliance with international quality management systems. In Hungary, a national hemovigilance program is under pilot study for reporting recipient-related data. In Thailand, national guidelines for blood safety and transfusion activities are implemented, ensuring compliance with international standards.
